d: Audiobook Studio is a local-first app that turns a manuscript into a finished, multi-voice audiobook using AI voice cloning — all on your own machine.
x: At a glance It runs on your computer ; your text and audio stay local unless you choose otherwise. It's a production surface , not one-click text-to-speech — you direct narration line by line. One default local engine means no accounts and no per-word cost. You assemble narrated chapters into a real audiobook file (M4B/MP3). A production tool, not a "read it aloud" button Most text-to-speech tools give you one voice and one pass. Audiobook Studio is built for the messy reality of a whole book: many characters, lines that need a second take, pronunciation you want to fix, and a finished file at the end. You stay in control of the result. Assign a voice to the narrator and a different one to each character, regenerate just the lines you change, and listen back as you go. What it does Multi-voice narration. Give the narrator one voice and every character their own. Voice cloning & a library. Build voices from samples; organize them with icons and tags. Targeted repair. Edit a line and regenerate only that segment — no charge. Assembly & export. Combine finished chapters into an audiobook file. Local-first by design Your manuscript, samples, and audio stay on your machine. The default voice engine runs locally, so you can narrate an entire book with no account and no usage meter. If you ever enable an optional cloud engine, that choice is explicit and clearly disclosed. Tip — Prefer to keep everything offline? You can. The local engine needs no network once it's set up. How the pieces fit together Project & chapters — your book, broken into chapters of text. Voices & casting — voices assigned to the narrator and characters. Generation — a managed engine turns assigned text into audio. Assembly — finished chapters become a single audiobook file. In 2.0, generation runs in a managed, crash-isolated TTS Server with installable engines. See Studio 2.0 at a Glance .

d: Studio 2.0 is a ground-up rearchitecture. The big idea: move synthesis into a managed, crash-isolated TTS Server , and make engines and voices first-class, installable pieces.
x: At a glance Managed TTS Server runs engines in a separate, supervised process. A task orchestrator replaces the old single worker loop. An engine registry and voice bridge keep voices independent of engines. Engines install from GitHub; voices come from a Hugging Face library. A managed TTS Server Synthesis no longer runs inside the app. A dedicated TTS Server process hosts the voice engines, manages GPU memory, and exposes a clean internal API. Studio supervises it with a watchdog and restarts it if it stops responding. An engine can crash without taking down the app or losing your work. A task orchestrator Work is scheduled, not improvised. Instead of one worker loop juggling everything, 2.0 uses an orchestrator that queues jobs, tracks progress centrally, and recovers cleanly after a restart. Completion is decided by validated artifacts, not loose files. Engine registry & voice bridge One boundary routes every synthesis request. The registry knows what engines are installed and what they can do; the voice bridge is the only path that hands a request to an engine. Because a voice's identity is kept separate from any engine's assets, the same voice can move between engines without being rebuilt. Tip — You can add, update, or swap engines without rewrites rippling into the queue, the editor, or your projects. Installable engines & a voice library Engines and voices are bundles you can install and share. Engines are GitHub repos you install like Stable Diffusion extensions (clone to install, pull to update). Voices come from a Hugging Face library with icons, playable samples, and rich tags. Coming with 2.0 — the engine browser, the Hugging Face voice library, and AI voice casting are part of the 2.0 rollout. What stayed the same The workflow you already know — projects, chapters, voices, generate, assemble — is intact. 2.0 changes the machinery underneath, not the shape of producing a book.

d: Audiobook Studio is for anyone producing long-form spoken audio locally — indie authors, narrators, hobbyists, and developers who want to build on top of it.
x: At a glance Built for whole-book production , not one-off clips. Iterate freely — fixing a line costs nothing to regenerate. Handles multi-character dialogue with distinct voices. Doubles as a local TTS backend you can automate. Who it's for Indie authors & self-publishers. Produce an audiobook of your own work at home, no studio time or per-word fees. Narrators & voice artists. Build and reuse voices, scale narration, keep audio on your own machine. Hobbyists & accessibility users. Turn fan fiction, web serials, notes, or documents into audio. Developers & integrators. Use the gateway API, write engine plugins, publish voices. What it's built to do Full-book production The whole point is the long haul. Chapters, characters, a queue that survives restarts, and assembly into a finished file. Iterative correction without per-edit cost Revising is free. Because the default engine runs locally, re-record a clumsy line as many times as you like. Change the text, regenerate that segment, move on. Multi-character dialogue Every character can sound like themselves. See Characters & Narrators for casting. Studio as a TTS backend It's also a local speech engine for your own tools. Through the gateway API, scripts and apps generate speech via the engines you've installed. Coming with 2.0 — the documented gateway API and installable engines make automation first-class. See TTS Gateway API . When it might not fit Studio is a production tool. For a single short clip with no editing, a simpler utility may be faster. Studio shines when there's a book's worth of work to manage.

d: Your manuscript, voice samples, and finished audio stay on your machine. Anything that leaves is optional, opt-in, and clearly disclosed.
x: At a glance The default engine is local — text and audio never leave your computer. Cloud engines are optional and off by default . When something would leave the machine, Studio tells you first . No accounts, no recurring usage cost to run locally. What stays local Everything, by default. With the local engine, your chapters, the voice samples you upload, and every rendered file are processed and stored on your own machine. You can work completely offline once setup is done. What leaves the machine — only if you choose Cloud engines are opt-in. Studio supports optional cloud voice engines (enabled with an API key), but none are installed or active by default. If you turn one on, the text to be spoken — and any reference audio that engine needs — is sent to that provider to generate the audio. Heads up — a cloud engine means some data leaves your device. Studio surfaces this clearly before you use one, and shows which engines send data off-machine. This is a deliberate trade-off you control, not a default. The Cloud Engines page explains each engine's data behavior. No silent fallback Studio won't quietly route your work somewhere else. If a local engine can't do something, it tells you — it does not silently fall back to a cloud service. What runs where is always visible. Data ownership & cost You own your files. Projects, voices, and output live in folders you can back up, move, or delete. No usage meter locally. The local engine has no per-word or per-minute charge. No account required to install and use the local workflow. Tip — For maximum privacy, simply don't enable any cloud engine. The local default covers full audiobook production on its own.

d: A quick, scannable tour of what Audiobook Studio can do. Each capability has its own deeper page later in the handbook.
x: At a glance Voices, variants, and cloning, organized in a real library. A reliable queue with progress and restart recovery. Assembly and export to M4B / MP3. Extensible: a plugin SDK and an external API. Voices, variants & cloning Build a voice once, reuse it everywhere. Create voices from audio samples, keep multiple variants, and identify them with icons and tags. Voices are independent of any one engine. See Voices and the Voice Lab . Queue, progress & recovery Long jobs are handled gracefully. Generation and assembly run through a queue with live progress and ETAs. If the app restarts, work recovers — completion is judged by validated audio artifacts, not by whether a file happens to exist. Assembly & export End up with a real audiobook. Combine finished chapters into an M4B (or MP3) you can keep, play on any device, and share — with editable metadata and chapter titles. Extensibility Plugin SDK. Wrap any TTS engine behind a small contract and publish it. External API. Use Studio as a local text-to-speech backend for your own scripts. Coming with 2.0 — installable engines from GitHub, a Hugging Face voice library, and AI voice casting. See Plugin SDK . Where to go next Ready to install? Head to Getting Started . Want the concepts first? Start with Core Concepts .

d: Before installing, make sure your machine meets a few basics. The local engine benefits from a GPU, but you can get started without one.
x: At a glance Works on macOS, Linux, and Windows . Python 3.11 , Node 18+, and ffmpeg. A CUDA GPU is recommended for fast local synthesis. Disk space for models and your audio output. Operating system Studio runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows. The easiest install path (Pinokio) is available on all three; see Installation Paths . Software Python 3.11 — the app and engine environments are built against it. Node 18+ — to build the frontend from source. ffmpeg — for audio assembly and format conversion. Note — If you install with Pinokio, it sets up most of this for you. Hardware A CUDA-capable GPU makes local synthesis much faster , but isn't strictly required to try the app. More VRAM lets heavier engines run comfortably. See Performance & GPU Tuning . Disk space Leave room for engine model downloads (fetched on first use) plus your projects and rendered audio.

d: There's more than one way to install Studio. Pick the one that matches how hands-on you want to be.
x: At a glance Pinokio — easiest, recommended for most people. From source — for developers who want direct control. A one-command launcher provisions everything. An optional demo library lets you explore immediately. Pinokio (easiest) Pinokio handles the local setup for you. It installs the app and its environment and can optionally add a demo library with sample voices so you can try the workflow right away. Best for most people. From source (developers) Clone the repository and run the launcher. This gives you direct control over files, scripts, and the dev workflow. The launchers provision a virtual environment, the engine environment, and build the frontend — see Launcher Scripts . Demo library option Either path can install a demo library — a small sample project and voices — so the app isn't empty on first launch. Tip — Not sure? Start with Pinokio. You can always switch to a source install later.

d: The launchers are the one command that gets Studio running. They provision everything the first time, then start the app.
x: At a glance run.sh (macOS/Linux) and run.ps1 (Windows). First run provisions the app venv, the engine environment, and the frontend build. Flags control setup-only, reload, and the port. What they do On first run, the launcher provisions everything. It creates the app's virtual environment, sets up the separate engine environment, and builds the frontend. On later runs it just starts the server. Common flags --setup-only — provision dependencies without starting the server. --no-reload — run without the auto-reload dev watcher. --port <n> — serve on a different port (default 8123). On Windows, run.ps1 exposes the same options. See Launcher Options for the full list. Note — The two environments are separate on purpose — see The Two Environments .

d: Studio uses two Python environments. Keeping them apart prevents the app and the heavy engine dependencies from fighting each other.
x: At a glance ./venv — the web app and orchestrator. ~/xtts-env — the heavier local-engine dependencies. Separation avoids dependency conflicts. Why two? The app and the local engine have very different dependencies. The local cloning engine pulls in large machine-learning packages that can conflict with the app's lighter stack. Isolating them keeps both stable. What lives where ./venv — the FastAPI app, orchestrator, and tooling. ~/xtts-env — the local engine and its model dependencies. The TTS Server (which hosts engines) runs against the engine environment, while the app runs in its own. See TTS Server & Watchdog . Tip — If engine dependencies ever get into a bad state, you can recreate ~/xtts-env without touching the app — see The XTTS Environment .

d: Once installed, starting Studio is a single command. The first launch does a little extra setup, then opens in your browser.
x: At a glance Start with the launcher; the app serves on port 8123 . First run downloads engine models and creates working folders. Open http://127.0.0.1:8123 in your browser. Start the server Run the launcher and wait for it to come up. Under the hood it starts the app ( uvicorn run:app ) and the managed TTS Server. When it's ready, open http://127.0.0.1:8123 . What happens on first run Model downloads. The local engine fetches its model the first time it's needed; this can take a while. Folders are created. Studio sets up its projects, voices, and working directories. Plugins are discovered. Installed engines are registered with the TTS Server. Note — First-run model downloads can look like a long pause. Progress is surfaced in the terminal so you can see it's working, not stuck. Next Take the 5-Minute Workflow Tour to make your first audio.

d: The demo library is an optional bundle of a sample project and voices, so the app has something to explore the moment you open it.
x: At a glance Optional — install it during setup or skip it. Includes a sample project and ready-made voices. Safe to remove later. What it includes A small, finished-style project plus sample voices. It's the fastest way to see how chapters, voices, generation, and playback fit together without building anything first. Installing it Pinokio can install the demo library as part of setup; from source you can add it during the guided setup. Either way it's optional. Removing it Delete the demo project and voices like any other — nothing else depends on them. Tip — New to Studio? Install the demo library, then follow the 5-Minute Workflow Tour using it.

d: Here's the whole workflow in one short pass — from an empty project to a finished chapter.
x: At a glance Create a project and add a chapter. Build or pick a voice and assign it. Generate, review, and fix any lines. Assemble into an audiobook file. 1. Create a project & add a chapter Start with a project (title, author), then add a chapter by pasting text or uploading a .txt file. 2. Build or assign a voice Pick a voice for the narrator. Use a demo voice, or build one in the Voice Lab . Assign characters their own voices if the chapter has dialogue. 3. Generate & review Generate the chapter and listen back. Watch progress in the queue . If a line needs work, edit it and regenerate just that segment. 4. Assemble the audiobook Assemble finished chapters into an M4B (or MP3). See Assemblies & Export . Tip — Using the demo library? Every step above works on the sample project right away.

d: Studio targets macOS, Windows, and Linux. This page lists the per-platform notes and a quick smoke test to confirm a healthy install.
x: At a glance Install & launch on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Pinokio install & launch flow. First-run smoke test to confirm everything works. Per-platform install & launch All three desktop platforms are supported. The launcher provides the equivalent flow on each ( run.sh on macOS/Linux, run.ps1 on Windows). Pinokio offers a guided install on each as well. First-run smoke test App starts and loads at http://127.0.0.1:8123 . The TTS Server starts and the default engine reports ready. Create the sample project, build/pick a test voice, and synthesize a short line. Relaunch the app and confirm your work is still there. Heads up — If first-run model downloads stall, check your network and disk space — large models take time on the first run. Platform notes Platform-specific prerequisites (e.g. build tools, GPU drivers) and any known limitations are tracked alongside the install instructions in the repository.

d: Everything in Studio fits into a simple hierarchy. Knowing the levels makes the rest of the app click.
x: At a glance Library → Project → Chapter → Segment → Chunk. Segments are lines/blocks; chunks are what the engine actually speaks. Each level owns different settings. The levels Library — all your projects in one place. Project — one book: chapters, characters, defaults, and output. Chapter — a unit of text you narrate and assemble. Segment / block — a line or passage, assigned to a voice. Chunk — the actual piece of text sent to the engine. Why chunks exist Engines work best on bounded pieces of text. Studio splits long segments into chunks under a character limit, synthesizes each, and stitches them back together. This keeps quality consistent and makes targeted re-generation cheap. Note — You mostly work at the project, chapter, and segment levels. Chunking happens automatically. What each level owns Projects hold defaults (like the narrator and output preset); chapters hold their text and assignments; segments hold per-line voice choices. See Project Workspace .

d: A project has one narrator by default, plus any characters you define — each mapped to a voice so dialogue sounds distinct.
x: At a glance Every project has a default narrator . Define characters and give each a voice and color. Assignment drives how each line is read. The default narrator Narration uses the project's default narrator voice. It's the fallback for any line not assigned to a specific character. Characters Define a character, give it a voice and a color, and assign its lines. Colors make it easy to see who speaks what at a glance in the editor. See Characters . How assignment drives rendering Each line is rendered in its assigned voice. Change an assignment and only the affected lines need regenerating. You can assign one line, one character, or all unassigned narration at once. Coming with 2.0 — AI voice casting can suggest a fitting voice for each character from your library, with a reason for every pick — you stay in control.

d: A voice in Studio is a small hierarchy of its own. Understanding it makes the Voice Lab straightforward.
x: At a glance A Voice is a reusable identity. A Variant is a tuned version of that voice for an engine. Samples are the audio a variant is built from. Voice identity is kept separate from engine assets. Voice vs variant A voice is the identity; a variant is a usable build of it. One voice can have several variants — for different engines, speeds, or styles. Samples & rebuilds Variants are built from sample audio. Add or replace samples and rebuild to improve a clone. Quality depends a lot on the samples — see Voice Cloning Quality . Engine-per-voice & portability A voice's identity (name, image, tags) is separate from its engine-specific assets. That's what lets a voice move between engines, and what makes voices portable as shareable bundles. Coming with 2.0 — voices become shareable bundles with an icon, a playable sample, and rich tags, published to a Hugging Face library. See Voice Icons & Tags .

d: Studio can route synthesis to more than one engine. They split into local and cloud, with one local engine installed by default.
x: At a glance Local engines run on your machine — XTTS is the only default install. Cloud engines are optional and need an API key (e.g. Voxtral). Composite synthesis mixes engines within a chapter. More engines can be added as plugins. Local engines The default engine is local and private. XTTS is the one engine installed out of the box; it runs on your machine with no account. See Local Engine (XTTS Default) . Cloud engines Cloud engines are optional and opt-in. You enable one with an API key; none ship by default. Voxtral is one example. See Cloud Engines . Composite synthesis A chapter can mix engines. Composite synthesis stitches output from multiple engines/voices into one chapter. See Composite Synthesis . Plugins add more Engines are installable. Beyond the default, you can add engines as plugins from GitHub. See the Plugin SDK .

d: Turning a chapter into audio is a pipeline of clear stages. Each one has a job, and progress comes from the stages reporting in.
x: At a glance Analysis → Queue → Synthesis → Bake → Assembly. Each stage has a defined job. Progress is reported centrally, not guessed. The stages Analysis — the chapter is split into segments and chunks. Queue — work is scheduled by the orchestrator. Synthesis — the engine generates audio for each chunk. Bake — chunks are validated and combined into segment/chapter audio. Assembly — chapters are combined into the final audiobook. Where progress comes from Progress is centralized, not improvised per screen. Stages report into the progress service, which broadcasts a single, consistent view with an ETA. See Progress Services .

d: Studio decides what's done by looking at validated artifacts, not by whether a file happens to exist. That's what makes reuse and recovery reliable.
x: At a glance Completion = a validated artifact , not a file on disk. Unchanged audio is reused , not re-rendered. Work recovers after a restart. Finished audio lives in an immutable cache. Validated artifacts vs file existence A stray file doesn't mean a segment is done. Studio records validated artifact metadata (duration, format, the request it satisfies) and treats that as the source of truth — so a half-written or stale file is never mistaken for finished work. Reuse of unchanged audio If a segment hasn't changed, its audio is reused. Editing one line doesn't re-render the rest of the chapter, which is what makes iteration fast and free. Restart recovery & reconciliation Studio reconciles state on startup. After a crash or restart, it checks artifacts against expected work and picks up where it left off. See Backups & Recovery .

d: XTTS is the default local engine: a private, on-machine voice-cloning engine that needs no account. It's the bundled example of a local engine.
x: At a glance The only engine installed by default . Runs locally — private and free to run. Clones a voice from samples into a reusable profile. A GPU makes it much faster. Why a local engine is the default Local-first means your audio never has to leave the machine. XTTS ships as the default so you can produce a full audiobook with no account, no API key, and no per-word cost. What XTTS is & GPU needs XTTS is a neural voice-cloning engine. It runs on CPU but is dramatically faster on a CUDA GPU. Its model is downloaded on first use; see First Run . Latents & the voice profile A clone is captured as a compact voice profile. XTTS turns your samples into latents that represent the voice; that profile is what gets reused for synthesis. Profiles are kept separate from a voice's identity so the same voice can carry assets for more than one engine. Strengths & tuning Quality depends most on your samples. Clean, consistent recordings clone best. See Voice Cloning Quality for heuristics, and Engine Settings & Verification to configure and test it.

d: Cloud engines are optional. You enable one with an API key; none ship or run by default. Voxtral (Mistral-hosted) is one example.
x: At a glance Optional and opt-in — off until you enable one. Enabled with an API key . Some data leaves your machine when used. Voxtral is one example of this kind of engine. Why cloud engines are optional Studio is local-first. Cloud engines exist for people who want a specific hosted voice or model, but they are never required and never on by default. Enabling a cloud engine with an API key Add the provider's API key in Settings to enable it. Until a key is present, the engine stays hidden. Voxtral, for example, is enabled with a Mistral API key. What data leaves your machine Using a cloud engine sends the text to be spoken (and any required reference audio) to the provider. Studio discloses this clearly. See Local-First & Privacy . Heads up — a cloud engine means data leaves your device. Review the provider's terms; Studio shows facts, it doesn't act as a legal gate. When to use one Reach for a cloud engine when you specifically want a voice or model it offers. For most local audiobook production, the default local engine is enough.

d: Composite synthesis lets one chapter use more than one engine or voice, stitched into a single, seamless result.
x: At a glance Mix engines/voices within one chapter. Studio stitches the output together. Formerly called “mixed” synthesis. When chapters mix engines Sometimes the best cast spans engines. A narrator on the local engine and a specific character on another, for instance. Composite synthesis handles that within a single chapter. How composite rendering stitches output Each segment is rendered by its assigned engine/voice, then combined in order. Because completion is tracked per validated artifact, segments from different engines assemble cleanly into one chapter. Note — Composite was previously called “mixed” synthesis; you may still see that term in older material.

d: Each engine carries its own settings and a self-test, so you can configure it and confirm it actually works before relying on it.
x: At a glance Settings are schema-driven — the form comes from the engine. Verify runs a real test synthesis. Engines report a clear status. Schema-driven engine settings Each engine declares its own settings. Studio renders the form from that schema, so an engine's options (models, keys, tuning) appear without hard-coding anything in the UI. Verification & test runs Verify runs a quick synthesis to prove the engine is working. Use it after setup or after changing a setting, and read the diagnostics if it fails. Enable / disable & status Engines show a clear status — ready, needs setup, or unavailable — so you know what will happen before you queue a job. Manage all of this in Settings .

d: Cloning quality comes mostly from your samples. A few habits make a big difference.
x: At a glance Sample quality matters most. Clean, consistent recordings clone best. Use variants to find the best result. Sample selection heuristics Use clear speech with little background noise. Keep tone and pace consistent across samples. Prefer a handful of good samples over many noisy ones. Recording quality factors Room noise, clipping, and inconsistent levels hurt clones. A quiet space and a steady level go a long way. See the recording guidance in the Voice Lab . Variant strategies Build variants and compare. Different sample sets or settings can produce noticeably different results; keep the variant that sounds best for your project.

d: Here's the short version of what changed from 1.x to 2.0 — what you feel day to day, and what developers gain.
x: At a glance Synthesis moved to a managed TTS Server . A real orchestrator runs the queue and recovery. Engines and voices are installable bundles . A plugin SDK and external API open Studio up. Headline changes A managed, crash-isolated TTS Server hosts engines. A task orchestrator replaces the old worker loop. Engine behavior is driven by plugin manifests, not engine-ID branches. Completion is decided by validated artifacts, not loose files. What users feel day-to-day More reliability and less lost work. Crashes are contained, progress is steadier, and restarts recover. Voices get icons and tags; playback and the editor are smoother. What developers gain Clean extension points. A five-method plugin SDK, installable engines from GitHub, shareable voices on Hugging Face, and a documented gateway API. See this section 's other pages for detail.

d: The big 2.0 changes are structural. Here's what moved and why each shift matters.
x: At a glance One-shot subprocess → managed TTS Server. Worker loop → orchestrator. Engine-ID branches → plugin manifests. Raw-file checks → validated artifacts. From one-shot subprocess to a managed TTS Server Synthesis runs in a long-lived, supervised process with a watchdog, instead of being spun up ad hoc. Engines can crash and restart without losing app state. From a worker loop to an orchestrator Scheduling, progress, and recovery are centralized. The orchestrator owns the queue and reconciliation rather than a single loop doing everything. From engine-ID branches to plugin manifests Behavior is declared, not hard-coded. What an engine supports comes from its manifest, so adding an engine doesn't mean adding special cases across the app. From raw-file checks to validated artifacts Completion is judged by validated artifact metadata. A file existing is no longer mistaken for finished work. See Artifacts, Reuse & Recovery .

d: Beyond the rearchitecture, 2.0 adds capabilities that weren't possible before.
x: At a glance Plugin SDK & external TTS API. Composite engine and project backups. Predictive progress and VCR playback. Voice tags & icons. Extensibility A plugin SDK and an external TTS API. Wrap engines and drive Studio from your own tools. See Plugin SDK and TTS Gateway API . Production features Composite synthesis across engines in one chapter. Project backups and disk-based recovery. Predictive progress with ETAs, and VCR-style playback in the editor. Voice library Voices gain icons and tags , making a real, searchable library. See Voice Icons & Tags . Coming with 2.0 — installable engines from GitHub, the Hugging Face voice library, and AI voice casting land as part of the 2.0 rollout.

d: Upgrading from 1.x? Here's what carries over and what changes.
x: At a glance Live state moves toward a database. Folder layout is tidied. Your projects and voices carry over. State: toward SQLite Durable data lives in SQLite, with live runtime state in state.json. Existing data is migrated forward. See State: state.json + SQLite . Folders & compatibility Storage is normalized into clear per-project folders. Compatibility shims keep older layouts working during the transition. What carries over Your projects, chapters, and voices come with you. The workflow is unchanged; the machinery underneath is what moved. In progress — exact migration steps are finalized as 2.0 lands; this page will get the concrete checklist.

d: Need to describe 2.0 to others? These are the benefit-framed talking points.
x: At a glance Reliability & recovery story. Extensibility story (plugins + API). Polish story (playback, progress, voices). Reliability & recovery “It doesn't lose your work.” Crash-isolated synthesis, a real queue, and restart recovery mean long jobs survive the bumps. Extensibility “Make it yours.” Install engines like Stable Diffusion, publish voices like a library, and drive Studio from your own scripts via the API. Polish “It feels finished.” Predictive progress, VCR-style playback, and a real voice library with icons and tags. Tip — For audience-tailored versions, see the site's For Developers and For Everyone pages.

d: A running record of shipped changes. The 2.0 line is summarized here; the full history lives with the project.
x: At a glance 2.0 highlights collected here. Patch lines noted as they ship. Full history in the repository. 2.0 highlights Managed TTS Server + watchdog. Task orchestrator, predictive progress, recovery. Plugin SDK, external TTS API, composite synthesis. Voice tags & icons; clearer first-run model-download progress. Recent patch lines Patch-level changes are recorded as they ship. Note — The authoritative, dated changelog is maintained in the repository and release notes.

d: Short definitions for the terms you'll see across the handbook.
x: At a glance Content terms: project, chapter, segment, chunk. Voice terms: voice, variant, sample, engine. Pipeline terms: task, job, artifact. Content Project — one book and its settings. Chapter — a unit of text you narrate and assemble. Segment / block — a line or passage assigned to a voice. Chunk — the bounded piece of text actually sent to an engine. Voices Voice — a reusable voice identity. Variant — a tuned build of a voice for an engine. Sample — audio a variant is built from. Engine — the component that turns text into speech. Pipeline Task — a unit of work the orchestrator schedules. Job — a queued instance of a task. Artifact — validated output (with metadata) that defines completion.

d: A quick reference for the formats Studio reads and writes.
x: At a glance Text in: plain text. Audio in: common sample formats. Audio out: WAV, MP3, M4B. Text inputs Chapters accept plain text — paste it or upload a .txt file. Audio inputs (samples) Voice samples use common audio formats. Clean recordings clone best — see Voice Cloning Quality . Outputs Studio renders to WAV internally and exports MP3 or M4B. M4B is the standard audiobook container with chapters. See Audio Guidance & Formats .

d: A fast reference for getting around Studio.
x: At a glance Main navigation map. Common actions. Where key features live. Navigation map Library → your projects. Project → Chapters, Characters, Assemblies, Backups. Voice Lab → build and manage voices. Queue → monitor jobs. Settings → defaults, engines, API. Common actions Create a project; add a chapter (paste or upload). Build/assign a voice; generate; review and fix lines. Assemble to M4B/MP3. Note — Detailed walkthroughs live in the User Guide .

d: The Library is your home base — every project lives here, ready to open or create.
x: In progress — the Library is being refreshed as part of Phase 12; the shape below is the near-term target. At a glance Grid & list views with sorting. Create a project with title, author, series, and cover. Open or delete projects. Browsing See all your projects at a glance. Switch between grid and list views and sort to find what you need. Creating a project Create a project with its title, author, optional series, and a cover. These double as audiobook metadata at export time. Opening & deleting Open a project to enter its workspace ( Project Workspace ), or delete ones you no longer need.

d: Open a project and you land in its workspace — the header for metadata, and tabs for everything inside.
x: At a glance Edit project metadata and cover. Sub-nav: Chapters, Characters, Assemblies, Backups. Set project defaults like the narrator and output preset. The header Edit the project's metadata and cover from the header. Title, author, series, and cover travel through to the finished audiobook. Sub-navigation Chapters — add and manage chapters. Characters — define characters and assign voices. Assemblies — combine chapters into output. Backups — snapshot and restore. Project defaults Projects hold defaults like the default narrator and output preset, which apply unless a chapter or line overrides them.

d: Chapters are the units you narrate and assemble. Add them by pasting text or uploading files.
x: At a glance Add a chapter by upload or paste. See status and stats per chapter. Reorder and delete. Adding a chapter Paste text or upload a .txt file. Each chapter becomes its own unit of work. Status & stats Each chapter shows its status and basic stats so you can see what's drafted, generated, or ready to assemble. Reorder & delete Reorder chapters to match your book and remove any you don't need. Order carries through to assembly.

d: Characters let dialogue sound distinct. Define them once, give each a voice and color, and assignment does the rest.
x: At a glance Create a character. Assign a voice profile/variant. Use color coding to scan who speaks. Create a character Add the characters that appear in your book. The narrator exists by default; characters cover everyone else. Assign a voice Give each character a voice (and variant). Their assigned lines render in that voice. See Characters & Narrators . Color coding Each character gets a color so you can scan a chapter and see who speaks which lines at a glance. Coming with 2.0 — AI voice casting can suggest a fitting voice per character from your library, with a reason — you confirm the picks.

d: Assembly is the finish line: turn your rendered chapters into a real audiobook file.
x: At a glance Assemble a project into one file. Download M4B and manage outputs. Edit descriptions and see stats. Assemble a project Combine finished chapters in order into a single audiobook. Chapter order and titles come from your project. Download & manage outputs Download the M4B (or MP3) and manage past outputs. M4B is the standard chaptered audiobook container. Descriptions & stats Edit the description and review stats like total duration before you publish or share.

d: Backups let you snapshot a project and roll back if something goes wrong.
x: At a glance Create a backup with a comment. Optionally include audio samples. Download, restore, or delete snapshots. Create a backup Snapshot the project, with an optional comment to remember why. Toggle whether to include audio samples (bigger, but complete). Restore & manage Download, restore, or delete snapshots. Restoring rolls the project back to that point. See Backups & Recovery for the bigger picture.

d: The editor is where a chapter comes together: assign voices, generate, and listen back, all in one place.
x: In progress — the editor is consolidating around a single Script tab in Phase 12; the description below reflects that target. At a glance Script tab: assign, batch-assign, generate, watch progress. VCR playback: play / pause / stop / next / previous. Edit tab: raw text with resync preview. The Script tab Assign voices and generate from one place. Assign a line, a character, or all unassigned narration at once, then generate and watch progress inline. VCR playback Review like a tape deck. Play, pause, stop, and jump to the next or previous line to audition your chapter quickly. The Edit tab Edit the raw text and resync. Fix wording, then preview how it re-splits before regenerating affected segments. Note — Older Production/Performance/Preview tabs are folding into the Script tab.

d: The Voice Lab is where voices are born: create them, add samples, test, and prepare them to share.
x: At a glance Create a voice and pick an engine. Manage variants and samples. Test, preview, and import/export voices. Create a voice & pick an engine Start a voice and choose the engine it builds for. The default local engine works out of the box. Variants & samples Variants — add, rename, move, set speed, and give test text. Samples — upload, manage, and rebuild to improve the clone. Quality depends on samples — see Voice Cloning Quality and the built-in Recording Guide prompts. Test, preview & share Test a voice with quick previews, then import or export voice bundles. See Voice Icons & Tags for identifying voices. Coming with 2.0 — export a voice as a shareable bundle and publish it to a Hugging Face voice library.

d: Icons and tags turn a pile of voices into a real, searchable library.
x: In progress — the voice library (icons, tags, search) is part of the Phase 12 / 2.0 rollout. At a glance Upload a 1:1 icon per voice. Tag voices (gender, age, accent, character, …). Search and filter by tag. Per-voice plugin settings. Voice icons Give each voice a square (1:1) icon. It shows on cards and pickers so voices are easy to recognize. Tags Tag voices by their qualities — class, gender, age, accent, tone, and free-form labels — so you can find the right one fast. The tag set is organized into simple sections. Searching & filtering Search and filter the library by tag. Rich, structured tags also power AI voice casting. Coming with 2.0 — voices published to Hugging Face carry the same icon, sample, and tags, and are discoverable by the audiobook-studio-voice tag.

d: The queue is mission control for background work — see what's running, what's next, and how long it'll take.
x: In progress — the queue UI is being refined in Phase 12; behavior below is the target. At a glance Queue stats and ETA. Per-job output metadata (duration). Reorder, pause/resume, and clear. Live updates over WebSocket. Watching progress See live stats and ETAs as jobs run. Progress comes from a central service, so the numbers are consistent across the app. See Progress Services . Controlling jobs Reorder, pause/resume, and clear jobs. Job history stays available for reference. Live updates The queue updates in real time over WebSocket — no refreshing to see the latest state.

d: Settings is where you configure Studio: general defaults, engines, the external API, and diagnostics.
x: At a glance General: safe mode, default engine/speaker. Engines: enable, configure, install/update, delete. API panel; About/diagnostics. General Set project-wide defaults like safe mode and the default engine/speaker. Engines Enable, configure, install, update, and delete engines. Updates surface here as a notify-only alert with per-engine and Update-all actions. See Engine Settings & Verification and Installing & Updating Engines . API panel Enable and manage the TTS Gateway API. See Gateway Overview . About / diagnostics Check versions and diagnostics when you need to confirm what's installed or troubleshoot.

d: What goes in, what comes out, and how to keep quality high.
x: At a glance Text and audio inputs. Internal vs output formats. Bitrate, normalization, and length tips. Inputs Text chapters are plain text; voice samples are common audio formats. See File Formats . Internal vs output formats Studio renders to WAV internally, then exports MP3 or M4B. Working in WAV keeps quality high until the final export. Quality tips Pick a sensible export bitrate for spoken word. Let Studio normalize levels for consistent loudness. Keep per-segment text within the engine's chunk limit.

d: Stuck? Start here. These are the issues people hit most and how to clear them.
x: At a glance Failed jobs & retries. Voice quality problems. Enabling an optional cloud engine. Long-sentence warnings. Failed jobs & retries Open the job in the queue and read its reason. Most failures are setup-related (engine not ready, missing dependency) and clear after a retry. Voice quality Poor clones usually trace back to samples. See Voice Cloning Quality . Enabling an optional cloud engine Add the provider's API key in Settings. Cloud engines stay hidden until a key is present. See Cloud Engines . Long-sentence warnings Very long sentences may be split for the engine. If you see a warning, shortening or re-punctuating the sentence usually helps.

d: Engines are plugins. They run inside the managed TTS Server, behind one small contract, so Studio never has to know an engine's internals.
x: At a glance Engines are discovered as folder plugins. They run in the TTS Server , isolated from the app. Behavior is declared , not hard-coded into Studio. Built-in and community engines use the same path. Folder plugins & discovery An engine is a self-contained folder. Studio discovers engines in the engines directory, validates each manifest, and registers it. Built-in engines go through the exact same discovery as community ones. Studio-owns vs plugin-owns Studio owns persistence and orchestration; the plugin owns synthesis. A plugin must not import app internals or write outside its folder and the requested output path. This keeps engines portable and safe. The declared-hook model What an engine can do is declared in its manifest. Chunk limits, progress parsing, resources, and settings come from metadata, so adding an engine never means adding engine-ID branches across the app. See manifest.json Reference and Engine Contract & Hooks .

d: A plugin is a small repo with a predictable layout. Here's what each part does.
x: At a glance manifest.json + the engine entry class. settings_schema.json for the settings UI. requirements.txt for dependencies. tests/ travels with the plugin. Layout tts_<engine_id>/ manifest.json # discovery + capabilities + distribution engine.py # the StudioTTSEngine implementation settings_schema.json # JSON Schema -> settings form requirements.txt # runtime dependencies README.md icon.png # shown in the engine browser tests/ # plugin-local tests + fixtures Why self-contained Everything an engine needs lives in its folder so it can be published as its own GitHub repo and installed with a clone. See the API for driving Studio, and Using the Template to start. Note — Heavy model weights are not committed to the repo — they download on first use, keeping the bundle small.

d: The manifest is the engine's contract with Studio. These fields drive discovery, capabilities, behavior, and distribution.
x: At a glance Identity: engine_id , entry_class , versions. Capabilities, languages, and resource profile. Behavior metadata (chunk limit, progress). A distribution block for install/update. Core fields Field Purpose engine_id Stable id; also the tts_<id> folder name. display_name Shown in the UI and engine browser. engine_version / min_app_version Semver; gates updates. entry_class Path to the engine implementation. resource_profile GPU/VRAM/CPU needs for scheduling. supported_languages / supported_voice_asset_types What it can do. requires_network Cloud engines disclose off-machine calls. Distribution block Engines install from GitHub by git clone and update by git pull. The distribution block carries the git_url , project , discovery topic , and an optional pin_ref . See Installing & Updating Engines . Behavior metadata Behavior fields (chunk limits, progress patterns, per-voice settings) let core behavior come from data — see Behavior Metadata .

d: An engine implements a small, published contract — five required methods, two optional.
x: At a glance info / check_env / check_request / synthesize / settings_schema . Optional: preview , shutdown . Same contract for built-in and community engines. The five required methods def info(self): ... # metadata for the registry def check_env(self): ... # can this engine run here? def check_request(self, r): ...# pre-flight validation def synthesize(self, r): ... # write audio to r['output_path'] def settings_schema(self): ... # JSON Schema for the settings UI Optional overrides preview(r) — lightweight preview (defaults to synthesize). shutdown() — cleanup on unload (defaults to no-op). Rules Engines run in the TTS Server, not the app. Don't import app modules, start background threads, or write outside the plugin folder and the requested output path. Voice-asset building goes through the same contract.

d: Instead of special-casing engines in Studio's code, engines declare their behavior as metadata. Studio reads it and adapts.
x: At a glance Chunk limit and split target come from the manifest. Progress is parsed from a declared pattern. Settings render from a JSON Schema with UI hints. Per-voice settings are declared, not hard-coded. Text chunking Each engine declares its text chunk limit. Studio splits long segments accordingly, so chunking adapts per engine without code changes. Progress parsing Progress comes from a declared pattern. Studio turns engine output into normalized progress events using metadata, not engine-specific parsing scattered through the app. Schema-driven settings Settings forms are generated from settings_schema.json , with optional UI hints. Engines can also declare per-voice settings. See manifest.json Reference .

d: Studio checks that a plugin matches the contract version it expects before trusting it.
x: In progress — contract-version checks are being finalized in Phase 12. At a glance A contract version (v1) defines the expected surface. Expected callables and signatures are verified. Checks run at load, before synthesis. Contract version The plugin contract is versioned. Studio knows which contract version it supports and validates plugins against it. What's checked Required callables must exist with the expected signatures. Validation happens at load, so an incompatible plugin fails fast with a clear reason instead of mid-job.

d: Plugins get what they need through a context object — never by importing Studio's internals.
x: In progress — the context contract is being finalized in Phase 12. At a glance plugin/core stays portable (no app imports). A context is passed into Studio-facing adapters. Persistence stays Studio-owned. Why portability matters The engine core must run without Studio. Keeping it free of app imports is what lets engines be extracted and run standalone — see Portable Core & Standalone Repos . The context Studio passes a context into the plugin's adapter layer for the services it's allowed to use. Studio still owns persistence and state.

d: Engines are built to live as their own repos and even run outside Studio from a CLI.
x: In progress — the standalone harness is firming up in Phase 12. At a glance Engine repo layout (XTTS as the example). A CLI entry point and dependency path. A standalone builder harness. Repo layout Each engine is a self-contained repo (XTTS is the worked example) that Studio installs via git. The same folder runs in Studio and on its own. CLI & harness A CLI entry point lets an engine run without the app , which is handy for development and testing. A builder harness helps package and verify a standalone engine.

d: Dev Mode is how you preview a plugin's UI and behavior inside Studio while you build it.
x: In progress — Dev Mode is being finalized in Phase 12. At a glance Preview the plugin's UI in Studio. Drive it with scenario fixtures from the plugin. Use it as you build. What it previews Dev Mode renders your plugin's settings and flows the way users will see them, so you can iterate without a full release loop. Scenario fixtures Plugins ship fixtures that drive the preview , giving deterministic scenarios to check against while developing.

d: Engines install like Stable Diffusion extensions: browse, clone, and update with a click. You can also import a zip directly.
x: In progress — the in-app engine browser is part of the 2.0 rollout. At a glance Browse the GitHub topic audiobook-studio-tts , or paste a repo URL. Install = git clone; update = git pull. Updates show as a notify-only alert in Settings → TTS Engines. Import a zip or delete an engine from the UI. Install Find an engine and clone it down. Studio validates the manifest and folder name before any code loads, then registers it. Heavy weights download on first use. Update Updates are notify-only. Settings → TTS Engines lists available updates with per-engine Update and Update all ; Studio never updates without your click. Import & delete You can also import an engine from a zip (for offline or private engines) and delete engines with a confirmation. Dependency installs show clear feedback. Heads up — third-party engines run code in the TTS Server. Studio shows a trust prompt naming the source before installing a community engine.

d: Don't start from scratch — copy the template and fill in the blanks.
x: At a glance Copy the engine bundle template. Update the manifest and settings schema. Implement the five contract methods. Steps Copy the engine bundle template into a new tts_<id> repo. Edit manifest.json (id, entry class, capabilities, distribution). Describe options in settings_schema.json and deps in requirements.txt . Implement info / check_env / check_request / synthesize / settings_schema . Add the GitHub topic audiobook-studio-tts so Studio's browser finds it. See Engine Contract & Hooks and Testing Your Plugin .

d: Tests travel with the plugin, so an engine repo proves itself wherever it lives.
x: At a glance Plugin-local tests/ are collected by pytest. A contract test checks the required surface. Fixtures and generated outputs live with the plugin. Plugin-local tests Keep tests inside the plugin folder. They're collected alongside the app's tests, so the engine is verified in place. The contract test A contract test confirms the engine implements the required methods with the expected behavior — the fastest way to catch a broken plugin. Fixtures Ship fixtures (and any generated outputs) with the plugin so tests are deterministic and self-contained.

d: Sharing an engine for others? Here's the bar it should meet.
x: At a glance Passes a security & safety review. Is stable and performs reasonably. Is self-contained and properly licensed. Security & safety Engines run code, so safety comes first. Respect the boundaries (no app imports, only write to allowed paths), and disclose any network use. Stability & performance It should work reliably and not hog resources. Declare an honest resource profile so scheduling can do its job. Self-contained & licensed Everything in the repo, with a clear license. Tests included, weights downloaded on first use, license stated in the manifest.

d: The gateway turns Studio into a local text-to-speech backend your own tools can call over HTTP, using the engines you've installed.
x: At a glance A local HTTP API for synthesis. Enable it in Settings. OpenAPI docs at /api/v1/tts/docs . What the gateway is It exposes synthesis over HTTP so scripts and apps can generate speech through Studio's installed engines — no cloud account needed. Enabling it Turn the gateway on in Settings . It's off by default. Once enabled, the interactive OpenAPI docs are served at /api/v1/tts/docs . Note — This is for an AI/automation audience — the endpoint pages are precise enough to hand to your own assistant to integrate.

d: Before exposing the gateway beyond localhost, lock it down with a key and rate limits.
x: At a glance Bearer API-key auth. Consider LAN binding carefully. Per-IP rate limiting. API key (Bearer) Authenticate requests with a Bearer token. Send Authorization: Bearer <key> on each call. curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $STUDIO_API_KEY" \ http://127.0.0.1:8123/api/v1/tts/engines LAN binding & rate limits Binding to a LAN address exposes the gateway to your network. Use the API key, apply per-IP rate limiting, and consider a reverse proxy. See Headless & LAN Exposure .

d: The gateway's surface is small. Here are the routes you'll use.
x: At a glance Discover engines. Synthesize and preview. Fetch job status and audio. Routes Method & path Purpose GET /api/v1/tts/engines List installed engines. GET /api/v1/tts/engines/{id} Details for one engine. POST /api/v1/tts/synthesize Synthesize text (inline or queued). POST /api/v1/tts/preview Quick preview synthesis. GET /api/v1/tts/jobs/{id} Poll a queued job's status. GET /api/v1/tts/jobs/{id}/audio Download a finished job's audio. See Inline vs Queued + Polling for how short and long text differ, and Examples for copy-paste calls.

d: How a request behaves depends on length: short text comes back immediately; long text becomes a job you poll.
x: At a glance Short text → inline audio in the response. Long text → a job id + poll URL. Poll until complete, then fetch the audio. Inline Below the inline threshold, synthesis returns audio directly. One request, one response — simplest for short snippets. Queued + polling Above the threshold, you get a job id and a poll URL. Poll GET /api/v1/tts/jobs/{id} until it's done, then download from /jobs/{id}/audio . POST /api/v1/tts/synthesize -> { "job_id": "...", "poll": "/api/v1/tts/jobs/..." } GET /api/v1/tts/jobs/{id} -> { "status": "running" | "done" | "failed" } GET /api/v1/tts/jobs/{id}/audio -> the audio file

d: When the gateway and the app both want the engine, a priority policy decides who goes first.
x: At a glance TTS_API_PRIORITY sets the mode. Modes: studio_first, equal, api_first. Designed to avoid starvation. The modes Mode Behavior studio_first Studio's own jobs take precedence over API jobs. equal API and Studio jobs share the queue fairly. api_first API jobs take precedence (for backend-style use). Avoiding starvation Whichever mode you pick, scheduling avoids starving the other side. Set the mode via the TTS_API_PRIORITY environment variable — see Environment Variables .

d: Concrete calls you can copy, paste, and hand to your own AI to wire up an integration.
x: At a glance Discover engines. Synthesize inline and queued. Poll and download audio. Discover engines curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ http://127.0.0.1:8123/api/v1/tts/engines Synthesize curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8123/api/v1/tts/synthesize \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"text": "Chapter one.", "voice": "gravel-road"}' Poll & download (long text) # returns {"job_id":"abc","poll":"/api/v1/tts/jobs/abc"} curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:8123/api/v1/tts/jobs/abc curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -o out.wav \ http://127.0.0.1:8123/api/v1/tts/jobs/abc/audio

d: Looking ahead: what an LLM or external controller would need to drive Studio, and where the gaps are.
x: Coming with 2.0 — this is planning only — not built yet. It captures the direction so the API can grow toward it. At a glance What a controller would need from the API. Gaps currently being verified. Direction, not a shipped feature. What a controller would need A controller needs to discover capabilities, submit work, and observe results — list engines/voices, synthesize, and poll jobs, all of which the gateway already covers in basic form. Current gaps Richer capability description and status detail are being verified as candidates for the controller surface. Nothing here is committed yet.

d: A map of the 2.0 subsystems and who owns what, plus how a request flows end to end.
x: At a glance Clear ownership: orchestrator, watchdog, voice bridge. A request flows app → bridge → TTS Server → engine. No import-time side effects. Ownership split Orchestrator — schedules and recovers work. Watchdog — supervises the TTS Server process. Voice bridge — the only route from a request to an engine. Request flow A synthesis request travels app → voice bridge → TTS Server → engine, and results come back as normalized artifacts and progress. See VoiceBridge and TTS Server & Watchdog . No import-time side effects Importing a module must not start servers, load models, or touch the filesystem. Startup happens in one explicit place — see Boot Sequence .

d: Synthesis runs in a separate, supervised process. If it dies, the watchdog brings it back.
x: At a glance A long-lived subprocess hosts engines. A READY signal marks it up. A watchdog spawns, health-checks, and restarts it. A circuit breaker prevents crash loops. The server process The TTS Server hosts all engines and manages GPU memory. It signals readiness once up, and Studio talks to it over HTTP via the bridge. The watchdog Studio spawns and supervises the server. It polls health, restarts on failure, and uses a circuit breaker so a persistently broken engine doesn't spin in a restart loop.

d: Every synthesis request goes through one place: the VoiceBridge. That's what keeps engine details out of the rest of the app.
x: At a glance Routes requests to engines over HTTP. A remote bridge + client talk to the TTS Server. Honors engine enablement and readiness. Routing The bridge resolves the voice, validates readiness, builds the engine request, and normalizes the result. Nothing else calls engines directly. Remote client A bridge client speaks to the TTS Server over HTTP. Studio caches engine info from the server rather than importing engine code. See Plugin Architecture .

d: The orchestrator owns background work: it submits, schedules, cancels, and recovers tasks.
x: At a glance A StudioTask abstraction with task types. Submit / cancel / recover operations. Policies, resources, and recovery rules. A job-handler registry. Tasks & jobs Work is modeled as tasks with explicit types. The orchestrator turns them into queued jobs and runs them under scheduling policies that respect engine resources. Recovery Recovery is built in. After a restart, the orchestrator reconciles what's done against what's expected and resumes. A job-handler registry maps job kinds to their handlers. See Progress Services and Artifacts, Reuse & Recovery .

d: Progress is computed in one place and broadcast, so every screen shows the same numbers.
x: At a glance One source for progress math. Rounded sensibly; broadcast on meaningful change. ETA estimation and reconciliation as truth. Centralized math Progress is calculated centrally and rounded (broadcasting only on meaningful change) to avoid noisy, inconsistent updates across screens. ETA & reconciliation ETAs come from observed throughput; reconciliation is the source of truth. What actually exists as validated artifacts wins over optimistic in-memory state.

d: Startup is deliberate and idempotent — and it's the only place side effects live.
x: At a glance boot_studio() and boot_tts_server() . Migrations run, then the watchdog starts. Idempotent and off the request path. Explicit startup Boot functions own all startup side effects. Migrations run first, then the watchdog brings up the TTS Server. Importing modules never triggers this. Idempotent Boot can run safely more than once and never happens as a side effect of handling a request — keeping requests fast and predictable.

d: Studio keeps fast-changing runtime state in a JSON file and durable data in SQLite.
x: At a glance state.json — live jobs and settings. SQLite — projects, chapters, segments, queue history. Moving toward a StorageManager. Live vs durable state.json holds live runtime state (in-flight jobs, settings), while SQLite holds durable data (projects, chapters, segments, queue history). Direction Storage access is consolidating behind a StorageManager so route handlers and tasks don't reach into paths directly. See Storage Layout .

d: The web layer is a FastAPI app: domain routers for the UI, a WebSocket for live updates, and the gateway mounted as a sub-app.
x: At a glance web.py mounts and lifecycle. Domain routers behind the UI. ws.py broadcasts live updates. Jobs moving from REST polling to WebSocket. App & routers FastAPI hosts domain routers (projects, chapters, voices, queue, and more) plus the external gateway as a mounted sub-app. See Internal HTTP API Reference and TTS Gateway API . Live updates A WebSocket broadcasts progress and state so the UI updates without polling; queue updates are migrating from REST polling to the WebSocket.

d: User-influenced paths are treated as hostile input. Studio contains them with dedicated helpers.
x: At a glance safe_join / secure_join_flat / find_secure_file . A containment pattern for all path building. Aligned with static analysis (CodeQL). Containment Never join user input into a path directly. The secure-join helpers keep resolved paths inside their intended root, blocking traversal. Why it matters Paths are an untrusted surface. Treating them consistently — and keeping aligned with CodeQL findings — prevents a whole class of vulnerabilities.

d: The UI is a React app with a clear split between canonical data and live overlays.
x: At a glance pages / components / hooks / store / theme. Canonical data vs live overlays. Tests under frontend/tests. Organization The app is organized into pages, components, hooks, a store, and theme. The store holds UI state; it is not a second source of truth for canonical data. Canonical vs live Canonical data comes from the backend; live overlays show in-flight progress. Keeping them distinct avoids the frontend drifting from server truth. Tests live under frontend/tests .

d: The UI is backed by internal domain routes. These are grouped by area.
x: At a glance projects / chapters / voices / queue. generation / jobs / settings / system. analysis / migration / engines. Route groups Content — projects, chapters, voices. Work — generation, jobs, queue. System — settings, system, engines, analysis, migration. Note — These are internal routes for the UI. For the external, documented surface see the TTS Gateway API .

d: The launchers cover everyday running and a few special cases via flags.
x: At a glance run.sh / run.ps1 flags. A generic plugin setup loop. Port and reload control. Flags --setup-only — provision without starting. --no-reload — disable the dev auto-reload. --port <n> — change the port (default 8123). Setup loop The launcher provisions the app and engine environments and installs plugin dependencies the first time. See Launcher Scripts .

d: Studio reads a handful of environment variables for storage roots, plugin locations, and behavior.
x: At a glance Storage roots and base directory. Plugin and plugin-data locations. Engine env, ports, and test-mode flags. Common variables Variable Purpose AUDIOBOOK_BASE_DIR Base directory for storage roots. PLUGINS_DIR / PLUGIN_DATA_DIR Where engines and their data live. XTTS_ENV_DIR Location of the engine environment. TTS_API_PRIORITY Gateway vs Studio scheduling mode. Note — Ports and test-mode flags are also configurable; see the app config for the full list.

d: Everything Studio writes has a place. Here's the layout.
x: At a glance Per-project folders for audio, text, output, and trash. Voices and plugin data have their own roots. Transient and trash areas are separate. Per-project projects/<id>/ audio/ text/ m4b/ cover/ trash/ Shared roots Voices and per-engine plugin data live in their own roots , with transient and trash areas kept apart from durable content. See State: state.json + SQLite .

d: The local engine lives in its own environment. Occasionally you'll update or rebuild it.
x: At a glance What lives in the engine environment. An update script keeps it current. Recreate it if dependencies go stale. What lives there The local engine and its heavy dependencies live separately from the app to avoid conflicts. See The Two Environments . Updating & recreating An update script refreshes the engine environment. If dependencies get into a bad state, recreate it without touching the app.

d: A few scripts help with stats, recovery, and development.
x: At a glance Backfill stats and sync durations. Recover projects from disk. Install hooks and a dev helper. Data maintenance Backfill / sync — recompute stats and durations. Recover — rebuild project state from files on disk. Development Hook installers and a dev helper streamline local development. See Testing & Verification .

d: Two layers protect your work: project backups you take, and automatic reconciliation on startup.
x: At a glance Project backups (optionally with audio). Disk-based project recovery. Startup reconciliation. Backups Snapshot a project and restore it later. See Backups for the in-app flow. Recovery & reconciliation Studio can rebuild project state from disk and reconciles state on startup so a crash doesn't lose validated work. See Artifacts, Reuse & Recovery .

d: You can run Studio on a machine and reach it from elsewhere — just secure it first.
x: At a glance Serve on a LAN address. Secure the gateway with a key + rate limits. Reverse-proxy notes. Serving on a LAN Bind to a network address to reach Studio from other devices. Doing so exposes it beyond localhost, so treat security as mandatory. Securing it Require the API key, apply per-IP rate limits, and consider a reverse proxy with TLS. See Authentication & Rate Limiting .

d: A few levers make local synthesis faster and steadier.
x: At a glance GPU/VRAM considerations. CPS auto-tuning and ETA. Large-book load performance. GPU & VRAM A CUDA GPU dramatically speeds local synthesis. More VRAM lets heavier engines and longer chunks run comfortably. Throughput & scale Studio auto-tunes characters-per-second estimates for accurate ETAs and is built to keep large books responsive. Declare honest engine resource profiles so scheduling avoids collisions.

d: Contributions follow a simple fork-and-PR flow with focused, reviewed changes.
